newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians aim to fix Mir before US Shuttle arrives.
newsitem.headline: Russians aim to fix Mir before US Shuttle arrives.

text.p: Two cosmonauts due to blast off for the crippled Mir space station hope to finish risky repairs before the U.S. space shuttle docks with it in September, a Russian space official said on Thursday.
Mission director Vladimir Solovyov said work to restore the power supply, damaged in a collision a month ago, would start soon after the cosmonauts arrive on Mir in August 7.

"In the first few days after the new crew gets to Mir, we plan to start restoring the power supply. I think it will work out before the shuttle arrives," he told reporters at Korolyov Mission Control outside Moscow.
"Scientific experiments, the main purpose of our missions and foreign missions to Mir, are pointless until the power supply is restored."
Solovyov was clearly responding to remarks on Wednesday by U.S. President Bill Clinton's top science adviser, Jack Gibbons.
Gibbons said Mir's power problems could could prevent U.S. astronaut Wendy Lawrence taking a turn on Mir. Her launch on the shuttle is scheduled for September 17.
Mir lost up to half of its power supply after a docking manoeuvre went wrong on June 25 and the Spektr scientific module attached to the station was punctured.

The crew had to urgently disconnect cables leading from the module to the rest of Mir to seal the hatch to the holed Spektr. British-born NASA astrophysicist Michael Foale was then forced to stop his scientific experiments.
NASA could decide whether to send Lawrence to Mir as late as the day before the shuttle is launched, Gibbons said.
Lawrence, a 37-year-old U.S. Navy commander, is in training at Zvyozdny Gorodok (Star City) outside Moscow for a four-month stint on Mir and is due to replace Foale.

The Russian relief crew, mission commander Anatoly Solovyov and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov, will put on spacesuits to enter Spektr to carry out the repairs. They trained on Thursday in a pool at Zvyozdny Gorodok, simulating the repairs.
They spent Tuesday and Wednesday at the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan inspecting the Soyuz TM-26 spacecraft that will blast off from there on August 5 and take them into space.
The three-man crew on Mir are preparing for their arrival.

"They have to clean up the station a bit, make preparations for better orientation in space for the new Soyuz to dock, and make all life support systems work under the bigger load they will have when five men are aboard instead of three," he said.
Solovyov said mission commander Vasily Tsibliyev, who has developed an irregular heartbeat, was still taking medicine despite an improvement in his condition.
But he said he would would be able to perform the landing after he and Russian flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin leave Mir on August 14 and return to earth.
He said Mission Control was not pinning the blame for Mir's recent problems on the cosmonauts and that they should not feel any psychological pressure.
In the jinx-like series of mishaps since the accident on June 25, an unidentified liquid leaked into space and one of the cosmonauts caused a computer to crash by pulling out a cable.
